title: Solar and Battery Rebates in San Diego 2026: $250 to $500 per kWh from Community Power | HomePowerRebate
desc: San Diego Community Power pays $350 per kWh for a battery with new solar, $250 for a battery added to existing solar, and more for CARE and FERA customers. Rules and steps.
h1: Solar and Battery Rebates in San Diego
lead: San Diego Community Power pays an upfront rebate of $250 to $500 per kilowatt-hour for a home battery, depending on whether you are adding it to new or existing solar and whether you qualify for the CARE or FERA rate. It also pays $0.10 per kWh for helping the grid on weekday evenings. Every rule below is the program's own.
cards_heading: What San Diego Community Power pays
cards_intro: These figures come from the Solar Battery Savings page of San Diego Community Power (SDCP), which we read on October 2, 2026. The page describes the 2025 program, and says people who joined the 2024 pilot have different rules. You must be an SDCP residential customer.

cards.title: New solar and battery, market rate
cards.note: Upfront rebate on the battery's capacity.

cards.title: Existing solar, new battery, market rate
cards.note: For adding a battery to a solar system you already have.

cards.title: CARE, FERA or Community of Concern
cards.note: $500 for new solar and battery and $350 for a battery on existing solar.

cards.title: Performance incentive
cards.note: Paid when the battery discharges 50% during the required weekday window between 4 p.m. and 9 p.m.

after_cards:
What the rebate looks like in dollars

A 13.5 kWh battery added to existing solar earns 13.5 x $250 = $3,375 at the market rate, or 13.5 x $350 = $4,725 for a CARE or FERA household. On a new solar and battery system the same battery earns $4,725 at the market rate and $6,750 at the higher rate. Performance payments come on top. SDCP's page says the amount depends on battery size and system type, and its program manual has the payment timeline.
sections: The program asks the battery to discharge at least 50% of its usable capacity during a weekday window that always falls between 4 p.m. and 9 p.m., to power your home and support the local grid. You can share extra stored energy with the grid afterward and receive your normal net metering payments or Solar Billing Plan export credits. The battery must be charged by your home's solar panels, not the grid, and it must be at a single-family home at the address where you receive service. You cannot also be in other demand response programs such as the Emergency Load Reduction Program or Demand Side Grid Support.

SDCP says to pick a contractor from its approved list, review approved battery models with them, and have the contractor submit your application to Community Power for approval before installation, reserving the rebate. After installation the manufacturer turns the battery on and it starts sending performance data. Installing first and applying later puts the rebate at risk, so do not let a salesperson start the work until the reservation is confirmed.

SDCP supplies your electricity if you live in the City of San Diego, and SDG&E delivers it and runs the wires. SDCP's page also tells customers about its Solar Billing Plan and rooftop solar rules. San Diego averaged about 5.3 peak sun hours a day (2020 to 2024), and its average January low was 8.8°C over 2015 to 2024, so a battery does not have to work hard against the cold. Compare with San Francisco, where the battery program is still marked coming soon, and SMUD's $300 per kWh.

Escondido customers buy power from SDG&E, not SDCP, so this rebate does not apply there. Renters and condo owners without their own single-family home with solar cannot use it. Check your electric bill for the name San Diego Community Power before you plan around it. Households at or below 80% of area median income in listed communities may qualify for no-cost upgrades through the Equitable Building Decarbonization program instead.
The federal 25C and 25D tax credits ended after December 31, 2025. SDCP's rebate is the main incentive for a San Diego battery today.
claim_heading: How to claim the SDCP rebate
claim_steps: Confirm that San Diego Community Power supplies your electricity and that your home is a single-family home.
Choose a contractor from SDCP's approved list.
Pick an approved battery model, and confirm it will charge from your solar only.
Have the contractor submit the application and reserve the rebate before installation.
Install the battery. The manufacturer turns it on and it starts sending data.
Earn the performance incentive when it discharges 50% in the weekday 4 to 9 p.m. window.
faq: How much does SDCP pay for a home battery?
$350 per kWh with new solar and $250 per kWh added to existing solar for market-rate customers. CARE, FERA and Community of Concern customers get $500 and $350.
Yes, $0.10 per kWh when the battery discharges 50% during the required weekday window between 4 p.m. and 9 p.m.
Can the battery charge from the grid?
No. The battery must be fully charged by your home's solar panels.
Do I apply before or after installation?
Before. The contractor submits your application for approval and reserves the rebate before installation.
Does the rebate apply in Escondido?
No. Escondido is not an SDCP member. Escondido customers buy electricity from SDG&E.
